1891:
Analogy Book — see every electrical idea as something you already know

The voltage is a pump, current is water flow, a resistor is a narrow pipe, a capacitor is a tank and an inductor is a heavy water wheel. This book gives a picture like that for 169 ideas across 19 subjects. Each card has the analogy, exactly how it matches the electrical behaviour, and the exam trap the picture helps you avoid.

How to use it: before solving a sum, say the picture out loud ("tank filling through a narrow pipe"). The picture tells you what cannot jump, what grows, what decays and which way things flow.

1893:
1. The water circuit — basic quantities

Voltage (EMF, potential difference) · V · volt

Picture it as: The PUMP (or the height difference between two tanks)

narrow pipe = R

pressure drop across the narrow pipe: V = I × R

PUMP = V water flow = current I (same all round a series loop)

How it matches: Pump pressure pushes water round the pipes; EMF pushes charge round the circuit. Voltage is always BETWEEN two points — like a height difference, never ‘at’ one point.

Exam use / trap: Voltmeter goes ACROSS (like a pressure gauge with two hoses); a node has potential only relative to ground.

Current · I · ampere

Picture it as: WATER FLOW rate (litres per second)

How it matches: Same flow passes every point of a single pipe — same current everywhere in a series loop.

Exam use / trap: Ammeter goes IN SERIES (cut the pipe and insert a flow-meter).

Charge · Q · coulomb

Picture it as: The WATER itself (total litres)

How it matches: Flow × time = litres; I × t = Q.

Exam use / trap: Q = It (TNEB 2018 Q57: 10 A × 240 s = 2400 C).

Resistance · R · ohm

Picture it as: A NARROW or ROUGH PIPE

How it matches: Long, thin pipes resist flow (R = ρL/A): longer pipe → more R, wider pipe → less R.

Exam use / trap: Stretch a wire n times → length ×n, area ÷n → R × n².

Conductance · G · siemens

Picture it as: How WIDE / EASY the pipe is

How it matches: G = 1/R — the opposite view of the same pipe.

Exam use / trap: Parallel conductances simply add (like parallel pipes adding capacity).

Power · P · watt

Picture it as: Pump pressure × flow = how fast the pump does work

How it matches: P = VI, like pressure × flow rate = hydraulic power.

Exam use / trap: Same pipe (series) → use I²R; same pressure (parallel) → use V²/R.

Energy · E · joule, kWh

Picture it as: Total work done lifting water

How it matches: Energy = power × time (E = Pt = VIt = QV).

Exam use / trap: 1 kWh = 1 unit = 3.6 MJ.
1894:
Ground / reference node · 0 V

Picture it as: SEA LEVEL

How it matches: All heights are measured from sea level; all node voltages from ground.

Exam use / trap: Changing the reference changes every node voltage, never the differences.

Short circuit · R = 0

Picture it as: A pipe with NO restriction (a bypass)

How it matches: All flow takes the free path; no pressure drop across it (V = 0, I anything).

Exam use / trap: Killed voltage source = short (pump removed, pipe joined).

Open circuit · R = ∞

Picture it as: A CLOSED VALVE / blocked pipe

How it matches: Pressure can exist across it but no flow (I = 0, V anything).

Exam use / trap: Killed current source = open. Ideal voltmeter = open.
1895:
2. Circuit laws

Ohm's law · V = IR

Picture it as: Pressure drop = flow × pipe narrowness

How it matches: Push harder → more flow; narrower pipe → less flow for the same push.

Exam use / trap: Holds for metals at constant temperature (not for diodes, arcs).

KCL · ΣI = 0

Picture it as: Water entering a JUNCTION = water leaving

How it matches: Water cannot pile up at a pipe joint; charge cannot pile up at a node.

Exam use / trap: Charge conservation.

KVL · ΣV = 0

Picture it as: Walk round a closed HILL path — total climb = total descent

How it matches: Back at the start you are at the same height; round any loop the rises equal the drops.

Exam use / trap: Energy conservation.

Series · Rs = R1 + R2

Picture it as: Pipes JOINED END TO END

How it matches: The same water passes both; each narrow section adds resistance.

Exam use / trap: Series: same I, voltage divides in proportion to R.

Parallel · 1/Rp = 1/R1 + 1/R2

Picture it as: Pipes SIDE BY SIDE (more lanes on a road)

How it matches: More lanes → easier flow → less total resistance, always below the smallest.

Exam use / trap: Parallel: same V, current divides in INVERSE proportion to R.

Voltage divider · Vout = V R2/(R1 + R2)

Picture it as: Pressure shared by two pipe sections

How it matches: The narrower section takes the bigger share of the pressure drop.

Exam use / trap: Loading the output (connecting a load) lowers it.

Thevenin equivalent · Vth, Rth

Picture it as: A pump with a built-in narrow pipe, seen from the tap

How it matches: Whatever the plumbing behind the tap, it looks like one pump (Vth) in series with one pipe (Rth).

Exam use / trap: Rth: kill sources (pump → plain pipe, current source → closed valve).

Superposition · —

Picture it as: Two people pushing the same trolley

How it matches: Effect of each pusher alone, added = total effect (only for linear systems).

Exam use / trap: NOT valid for power (power ∝ I², not linear).

Maximum power transfer · RL = Rth

Picture it as: Water wheel loaded just right

How it matches: Too little load: water rushes past doing nothing; too much: flow nearly stops. Best when load matches the source pipe.

Exam use / trap: Efficiency at max power is only 50 %.

Dependent source · —

Picture it as: A pump whose speed is set by a sensor elsewhere

How it matches: Its push depends on another flow/pressure in the circuit.

Exam use / trap: Never ‘kill’ a dependent source when finding Rth — use a test source.
1896:
3. Capacitor, inductor and transients

Capacitor · C · farad

Picture it as: A TANK (or a balloon / spring diaphragm)

TANK = capacitor C

Filling slows as the level rises:

63 % full at t = τ = RC, ~99 % at 5τ.
The level cannot jump instantly → capacitor voltage is continuous.level = v_C

narrow pipe = R

pump = source V

How it matches: Charging = filling the tank; the fuller it is, the harder it pushes back. A big tank (big C) needs more water (Q = CV) to rise 1 m.

Exam use / trap: Voltage across C cannot JUMP (tank level can't change instantly). In DC steady state the full tank stops the flow → C = open.

Inductor · L · henry

Picture it as: A HEAVY WATER WHEEL / long pipe full of moving water (inertia)

HEAVY WHEEL = inductor L

flow = current i — the heavy wheel resists any CHANGE of flow

shut the valve suddenly → water hammer (big voltage spike L di/dt)

How it matches: Moving water resists any change in flow — it keeps going when the pump stops (water hammer).

Exam use / trap: Current through L cannot JUMP. In DC steady state the wheel turns freely → L = short.

Time constant RC · τ = RC

Picture it as: Time to fill a tank through a narrow pipe

How it matches: Bigger tank (C) or narrower pipe (R)

→ slower filling. After 1τ the tank is 63 % full, after 5τ practically full.

Exam use / trap: Find t: t = τ ln(…) — take ln of the exponential.

Time constant L/R · τ = L/R

Picture it as: Time for a heavy wheel to spin up against friction

How it matches: Heavier wheel (L) → slower; more friction (R) → settles faster (smaller τ).

Exam use / trap: Note the INVERSE: more R makes RL faster but RC slower.
1897:
Energy in C · ½CV²

Picture it as: Water stored HIGH in the tank (potential energy)

How it matches: Energy sits in the electric field like water held up.

Exam use / trap: Halving V leaves ¼ of the energy.

Energy in L · ½LI²

Picture it as: Energy of the MOVING water (kinetic energy)

How it matches: Energy is in the magnetic field like momentum in a moving mass.

Exam use / trap: Opening an inductive circuit suddenly → huge spark (water hammer).

LC oscillation · ω₀ = 1/√(LC)

Picture it as: Water sloshing in a U-TUBE (or a pendulum, a mass on a spring)

high side

= C full

How it matches: Tank (C) stores height energy, moving water (L) stores motion energy; energy swaps back and forth.

Exam use / trap: With no R it rings for ever; R = friction makes it die out.

Initial value (t = 0⁺) · —

Picture it as: Tank level / wheel speed just after the switch

How it matches: Neither can change in zero time, so they equal their values just before switching.

Exam use / trap: vC(0⁺) = vC(0⁻), iL(0⁺) = iL(0⁻).
1898:
4. AC circuits

Alternating current · f · hertz

Picture it as: A SAW cutting wood — back and forth, yet it still does work

How it matches: Water sloshing to and fro in a pipe can still turn a paddle.

Exam use / trap: Average of a full sine = 0, but power is not zero.

RMS value · Vrms = Vm/√2

Picture it as: The STEADY push that would heat the same kettle

How it matches: 230 V rms AC heats a heater exactly like 230 V DC.

Exam use / trap: 230 V rms = 325 V peak. Meters read rms (MI) or average × 1.11 (PMMC rectifier).

Phase / phase angle · φ

Picture it as: Two children on SWINGS, one starting a little later

How it matches: Same rhythm (frequency), different timing (phase).

Exam use / trap: Compare phases only at the same frequency and same sin/cos reference.

Reactance XL · XL = 2πfL

Picture it as: Heavy wheel resists FAST back-and-forth more

How it matches: Faster sloshing (higher f) → the inertia fights harder.

Exam use / trap: XL ∝ f: zero at DC (short), huge at high f.

Reactance XC · XC = 1/(2πfC)

Picture it as: A rubber diaphragm in the pipe — easy for fast wiggles, blocks steady flow

How it matches: Steady flow (DC) is stopped; fast back-and-forth passes easily.

Exam use / trap: XC ∝ 1/f: open at DC, short at very high f.

Impedance · Z = R + jX

Picture it as: Total opposition = friction + inertia/spring effects

How it matches: R wastes energy as heat; X only stores and returns it.

Exam use / trap: |Z| = √(R² + X²); angle = tan⁻¹(X/R).

Power factor · pf = cos φ

Picture it as: A HORSE pulling a barge from the river bank at an angle

pf = cos φ = P/S

sideways = Q

useful pull = P

How it matches: Only the pull along the canal moves the barge (real power); the sideways pull is wasted effort (reactive).

Exam use / trap: Low pf → more current for the same useful power → bigger losses and cables.
1899:
Real, reactive, apparent power · P, Q, S

Picture it as: A glass of BEER: liquid = P, foam = Q, whole glass = S

foam = Q (kVAr)

whole glass = S (kVA)

S² = P² + Q² beer = P (kW)

How it matches: You pay for the whole glass (S) but drink only the beer (P). S² = P² + Q².

Exam use / trap: kW does work; kVAr only sloshes back and forth; kVA sizes the equipment.

pf correction (capacitor) · Qc = P(tan φ1 − tan

φ2)

Picture it as: Letting a SECOND horse pull from the other bank

How it matches: The sideways pulls cancel, so less total effort for the same forward motion.

Exam use / trap: Capacitor supplies kVAr locally; motors draw lagging kVAr.

Resonance · XL = XC

Picture it as: Pushing a SWING at exactly its natural rhythm

pushing at the natural

frequency f₀ builds a huge

swing = RESONANCE (high Q)

small push

exactly in step

How it matches: Small pushes in step build a huge swing; series resonance gives max current, parallel gives min current.

Exam use / trap: f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)); Q factor = how high the swing builds.

Q factor / bandwidth · Q = f₀/BW

Picture it as: A wine glass that rings for a long time (sharp tuning)

How it matches: High Q → rings long and responds only near one frequency (narrow bandwidth).

Exam use / trap: R raises losses → lowers Q → wider band.

Coupled coils / mutual inductance · M =

k√(L1L2)

Picture it as: Two water wheels on ONE shared axle (or two gears in mesh)

How it matches: Turning one drives the other; how tightly they are linked is k (0 to 1).

Exam use / trap: Aiding +2M (both currents into the dots), opposing −2M.
1900:
Reflected impedance · (ωM)²/Z2

Picture it as: A load on the second wheel makes the first wheel feel heavier

How it matches: Whatever the secondary carries is felt back on the primary.

Exam use / trap: Zin = Z1 + (ωM)²/Z2.
1901:
5. Three-phase

Three-phase supply · 120° apart

Picture it as: THREE CYCLISTS on one crank, pedals 120° apart

How it matches: Someone is always pushing hard, so the shaft gets smooth, constant power.

Exam use / trap: Balanced 3-φ: instantaneous total power is constant.

Neutral current · In = 0 (balanced)

Picture it as: Three equal pushes at 120° cancel exactly

How it matches: Like three equal ropes pulling a ring at 120° — the ring does not move.

Exam use / trap: Unbalanced load → neutral current flows; broken neutral → voltage shift.

Star vs delta · VL = √3 Vph (Y), IL = √3 Iph (Δ)

Picture it as: Star = meeting at a common hub; delta = holding hands in a ring

How it matches: Star adds two phases at 120° → √3 more voltage between lines; delta splits line current between two phases.

Exam use / trap: Star–delta starter cuts starting current to ⅓.

Phase sequence · RYB

Picture it as: The ORDER in which cyclists push

How it matches: Swap any two and the shaft turns the other way.

Exam use / trap: Swapping two supply lines reverses an induction motor.
1902:
6. Magnetic circuits and transformers

Magnetic flux · Φ · weber

Picture it as: WATER FLOW in a magnetic ‘pipe’ (the iron core)

How it matches: MMF pushes flux round the core like a pump pushes water.

Exam use / trap: Φ = MMF/reluctance — the ‘Ohm's law’ of magnetism.

MMF · NI · ampere-turn

Picture it as: The PUMP of the magnetic circuit

How it matches: More turns or more current → more push for flux.

Reluctance · S = l/(μA)

Picture it as: Narrow pipe for flux; an AIR GAP is like a sudden clogged section

How it matches: Even a small air gap dominates the total reluctance (air μ is ~1000× lower).

Exam use / trap: Machines need much more magnetising current than transformers because of the air gap.

Hysteresis · Ph ∝ f B^1.6

Picture it as: Bending a paper-clip back and forth — it warms up

How it matches: Magnetic domains flipping every cycle waste energy as heat.

Exam use / trap: ∝ f; reduced by silicon steel (narrow loop).

Eddy currents · Pe ∝ f²B²t²

Picture it as: Little WHIRLPOOLS in a river

How it matches: Circulating currents in solid iron waste energy; slicing the core (laminations) breaks the whirlpools.

Exam use / trap: ∝ f² and ∝ thickness²: laminate thin.
1903:
Referring impedance · Z′ = a²Z

Picture it as: Looking at a load through a gearbox

How it matches: Through gears the load ‘feels’ heavier or lighter by the ratio squared.

Exam use / trap: Refer to HV side: multiply by a²; to LV side: divide.

Open-circuit / short-circuit test · Pi, Pcu

Picture it as: Engine idling (fuel just to keep running) vs. braking at full load

How it matches: OC test at rated V shows core (idling) loss; SC test at rated I shows copper (load) loss.

Exam use / trap: OC on LV side, SC on HV side.

Maximum efficiency · Cu loss = iron loss

Picture it as: A shop whose fixed rent equals its variable costs

How it matches: Below that load the fixed cost dominates; above it the variable cost grows as x².

Exam use / trap: x = √(Pi/Pcu,FL).

Voltage regulation · (E − V)/V

Picture it as: Water pressure falling at the far tap when many taps are open

How it matches: Internal drop I(R cos φ + X sin φ) lowers the terminal voltage on load.

Exam use / trap: Leading pf can make regulation negative.

Current transformer · secondary never open

Picture it as: A water hose kinked under full pump pressure

How it matches: Primary current is forced by the line; opening the secondary removes the opposing flux → dangerous high voltage.

Exam use / trap: Always short a CT secondary before removing the meter.

Autotransformer · one shared winding

Picture it as: A STEP-LADDER instead of two separate ladders

How it matches: Part of the same winding serves both sides, so less copper.

Exam use / trap: No isolation between primary and secondary.
1904:
7. DC machines

DC motor · T = kΦIa

Picture it as: A water wheel turned by a pressure jet

How it matches: Current in a magnetic field gets a push (motor action).

Exam use / trap: Torque ∝ flux × armature current.

Back EMF · Eb = V − IaRa

Picture it as: A water wheel acting as a pump against the supply as it speeds up

How it matches: Faster spin → more back-push → less current. At start Eb = 0 → huge current (needs a starter).

Exam use / trap: Eb ∝ ΦN.

Speed vs field · N ∝ Eb/Φ

Picture it as: A cyclist on an easier gear spins faster

How it matches: Weaker field → needs to spin faster to make the same back EMF.

Exam use / trap: Field circuit open on a shunt motor

→ dangerous over-speed.

Series motor · T ∝ Ia²

Picture it as: A tug-boat — huge pull from standstill

How it matches: High starting torque (traction, cranes); runs away with no load.

Exam use / trap: Never start a series motor without load.

Commutator · —

Picture it as: A ROTATING SWITCH that flips connections each half turn

How it matches: Keeps the torque in one direction by reversing coil current at the right moment.

Armature reaction · —

Picture it as: A strong cross-wind bending a fountain jet

How it matches: Armature flux distorts and weakens the main field.

Exam use / trap: Interpoles and compensating windings correct it.
1905:
8. Induction and synchronous machines

Rotating magnetic field · Ns = 120f/P

Picture it as: A STADIUM WAVE running round the crowd

How it matches: Three phases in turn create a field that travels round the stator.

Exam use / trap: Swap two phases → wave runs the other way.

Induction motor torque–slip · Tmax at s = R2/X2

Picture it as: Dragging a boat with a rope through water

How it matches: Small slip: torque ∝ s; large slip: rotor reactance makes torque fall.

Exam use / trap: Adding rotor resistance moves Tmax to higher slip (more starting torque).

Synchronous machine load angle · P = (EV/X) sin δ

Picture it as: A DOG ON A LEASH beside its owner

owner = rotor (E)

same speed, angle grows with load; past 90° the

leash slips (out of step)

dog = bus (V)

How it matches: Both run at the same speed; harder pull → bigger angle δ; past 90° the leash slips (loss of synchronism).

Exam use / trap: Pmax at δ = 90°.
1906:
Over/under excitation · —

Picture it as: Adjusting how hard the dog leans sideways

How it matches: Over-excited synchronous motor supplies kVAr (works like a capacitor); under-excited draws kVAr.

Exam use / trap: Synchronous condenser = over-excited motor on no load.

Synchronising (paralleling) · same V, f, phase,

sequence

Picture it as: Jumping onto a moving merry-go-round

How it matches: Match speed and position first, then step on smoothly.

Exam use / trap: Dark-lamp / synchroscope method.

Single-phase induction motor · needs auxiliary

winding

Picture it as: A pendulum pushed straight — it swings but chooses no direction

How it matches: A single winding gives a pulsating field (two equal opposite waves) → no starting torque.

Exam use / trap: Capacitor-start adds a second phase-shifted field.
1907:
9. Power systems

Transmission at high voltage · loss = I²R

Picture it as: Sending water through pipes at HIGH PRESSURE, LOW FLOW

How it matches: Same power with less current → much less friction loss in long pipes.

Exam use / trap: Double the voltage → quarter the loss.

Power flow P = V1V2 sin δ / X · δ

Picture it as: Water flows from the HIGHER tank to the lower (angle = height)

How it matches: Real power flows from the leading angle to the lagging; reactive power flows from higher V to lower V.

Exam use / trap: Pmax = V1V2/X at 90°.

Voltage drop / reactive power · Q ↔ V

Picture it as: Pressure falling at the end of a long pipe

How it matches: Reactive power support (capacitors) props up the pressure (voltage) locally.

Exam use / trap: Q controls V; P controls f and δ.

Ferranti effect · Vr > Vs on light load

Picture it as: A water-hammer / sloshing rise at the dead end of a long pipe

How it matches: Line charging current through line inductance raises the far-end voltage at no load.

Exam use / trap: Long lines on light load; shunt reactors fix it.

Frequency & load balance · f ↔ P

Picture it as: Keeping a bicycle's speed steady going up and down hills

How it matches: More load (uphill) → generators slow (f falls) until governors add more steam/water.

Exam use / trap: Droop: Δf ∝ ΔP.

Inertia constant H · H = stored KE / rating

Picture it as: A heavy FLYWHEEL that resists speed change

How it matches: Bigger H → frequency changes more slowly after a disturbance.

Exam use / trap: Swing equation M d²δ/dt² = Pm − Pe.

Transient stability (equal area) · A1 = A2

Picture it as: A ball rolling in a valley, kicked by a fault

How it matches: Energy gained during the fault (A1) must be given back before it rolls over the hill (A2).

Exam use / trap: Clear faults fast → smaller A1.

Per-unit system · pu = actual/base

Picture it as: Marks out of 100 instead of raw marks

How it matches: Everything on one common scale, so transformer ratios disappear.

Exam use / trap: Zbase = kV²/MVA.

Short-circuit fault · If = E/Z

Picture it as: A pipe BURSTING straight to the drain

How it matches: Flow is limited only by the pipe narrowness up to the break → enormous current.

Exam use / trap: 3-φ fault is usually the largest; LG most common.

Symmetrical components · +, −, 0 sequence

Picture it as: Breaking an untidy push into three neat patterns

How it matches: Any unbalanced set = a forward set + a reverse set + an in-step set.

Exam use / trap: Zero sequence needs a path to earth (neutral).
1908:
Earthing · low earth resistance

Picture it as: A big DRAIN to the ground

How it matches: Fault current has an easy path away, so touching the body stays safe.

Exam use / trap: Earth resistance should be low (≤ 1 Ω substations).

Corona · above disruptive voltage

Picture it as: Air ‘boiling’ around a too-thin, too-highly-stressed wire

How it matches: Air near the conductor ionises: hissing, glow, loss, radio noise.

Exam use / trap: Bundled / thicker conductors reduce it.
1909:
10. Protection and switchgear

Fuse · —

Picture it as: The WEAKEST LINK in a chain

How it matches: It breaks deliberately to save everything else.

Exam use / trap: Has to be replaced after operating.

Circuit breaker · —

Picture it as: A TAP that can shut under full flow and be reopened

How it matches: Opens contacts and quenches the arc; reusable.

Exam use / trap: Arc quenching media: air, oil, SF₆, vacuum.

Relay · —

Picture it as: A WATCHMAN who rings the bell for the breaker

How it matches: Senses abnormal current/voltage and tells the breaker to trip.

Exam use / trap: Relay detects; breaker interrupts.

IDMT relay · t ∝ 1/(PSM^0.02 − 1)

Picture it as: A guard who reacts faster to bigger trouble

How it matches: Large fault → quick trip; small overload → slow trip.

Exam use / trap: Grading: upstream relay waits a margin longer.

Differential protection · Iin = Iout

Picture it as: Counting people entering and leaving a hall

How it matches: If the counts differ, someone is trapped inside → internal fault.

Exam use / trap: Through faults do not trip it.

Distance relay · Z = V/I

Picture it as: Estimating how far a thunderclap is from the flash-to-sound time

How it matches: Measured impedance tells how far away the fault is.

Exam use / trap: Zones 1-2-3 cover more line with more delay.

Lightning arrester · —

Picture it as: A pressure-relief VALVE

How it matches: Stays shut at normal voltage, opens to bleed a surge to earth, then closes.
1910:
11. Power electronics

Diode · —

Picture it as: A NON-RETURN VALVE

How it matches: Lets flow pass one way only.

Exam use / trap: Forward drop ≈ 0.7 V (Si); reverse = blocks.

SCR (thyristor) · —

Picture it as: A LATCHING DOOR that opens on a knock and stays open while people pass

How it matches: A gate pulse turns it on; it stays on until current falls below holding current.

Exam use / trap: Gate can't turn it off (except GTO).

MOSFET / IGBT switch · —

Picture it as: A TAP that can be opened and closed on command, very fast

How it matches: Fully controlled switches for choppers and inverters.

Exam use / trap: MOSFET fastest, IGBT for higher power.

Rectifier · AC → DC

Picture it as: A NON-RETURN VALVE on a sloshing pipe

How it matches: Lets only one direction through, so the average flow moves one way.

Exam use / trap: Full-wave Vavg = 2Vm/π.

Firing angle α · Vdc ∝ cos α

Picture it as: Opening a SLUICE GATE later in each wave

How it matches: The later you open, the less water gets through each cycle.

Exam use / trap: α > 90° → average reverses (inverter mode).

Filter capacitor · ripple

Picture it as: A WATER TANK smoothing a pulsing supply

How it matches: Stores water at the peaks and supplies it between them.

Exam use / trap: Bigger C or load current smaller → less ripple.

Buck converter · Vo = DVs

Picture it as: A tap switched ON and OFF quickly — the average flow is less

How it matches: On for D of the time → average pressure D·Vs (the inductor smooths it).

Boost converter · Vo = Vs/(1 − D)

Picture it as: A HYDRAULIC RAM pump — the moving water's momentum lifts water higher

How it matches: The inductor builds momentum while shorted, then forces it out at a higher voltage.

Exam use / trap: D → 1 gives very high gain (in theory).

Inverter · DC → AC

Picture it as: Two people alternately pushing a door from each side

How it matches: Switches reverse the connection to make alternating output.

Exam use / trap: PWM shapes it towards a sine.

Freewheeling diode · —

Picture it as: A bypass pipe that lets moving water keep circulating

How it matches: Gives inductive current a path when the switch opens, avoiding a voltage spike.
1911:
12. Electronics

Semiconductor doping · n/p type

Picture it as: A queue with extra people (n) or empty seats moving along (p, holes)

How it matches: Electrons are the extra people; holes are gaps that appear to move the other way.

PN junction / depletion layer · —

Picture it as: A no-man's-land between two crowds

How it matches: Forward bias shrinks it (crowds pushed together); reverse bias widens it.

Zener diode · Vz

Picture it as: An overflow WEIR — water above the edge spills away

How it matches: Holds the voltage at Vz by passing whatever extra current is needed.

Exam use / trap: Used as a voltage regulator in reverse breakdown.

BJT transistor · Ic = βIb

Picture it as: A small hand turning a big WATER TAP

How it matches: A small base current controls a much larger collector current.

Exam use / trap: Saturation = tap fully open; cut-off = closed.

FET · voltage-controlled

Picture it as: A gate valve moved by PRESSURE, not flow

How it matches: Gate voltage controls the channel with almost no gate current (very high input impedance).

Amplifier gain · A = Vout/Vin

Picture it as: A MEGAPHONE

How it matches: Small input, bigger copy at the output, using power from a supply.

Exam use / trap: Gain in dB = 20 log(V ratio).

Negative feedback · A/(1 + Aβ)

Picture it as: A driver correcting the steering continuously

How it matches: Compares output with target and corrects → stable, accurate, less distortion, lower gain.

Exam use / trap: Gain × bandwidth stays constant.

Op-amp (ideal) · V+ = V−

Picture it as: A servant who adjusts the output until both inputs are equal

How it matches: With negative feedback it forces the virtual short; inputs draw no current.

Exam use / trap: Inverting gain −Rf/Rin.

Oscillator · Aβ = 1

Picture it as: A SWING kept going by tiny pushes in step

How it matches: Positive feedback in phase replaces the energy lost each cycle.

Exam use / trap: Barkhausen: loop gain 1, phase 0°/360°.

Logic gates · AND / OR

Picture it as: AND = two switches in SERIES (both must close); OR = in PARALLEL

How it matches: A lamp lights only if both (AND) or either (OR) switch is closed.

Exam use / trap: NAND/NOR are universal.

Flip-flop · 1-bit memory

Picture it as: A LIGHT SWITCH that stays where you left it

How it matches: Holds its state until told to change.
1912:
13. Control systems

Open loop vs closed loop · —

Picture it as: Toaster timer vs room THERMOSTAT

How it matches: Open loop does not check the result; closed loop measures and corrects.

Exam use / trap: Closed loop: accurate, can become unstable.

Steady-state error · ess

Picture it as: A cruise control that settles slightly below the set speed

How it matches: Proportional control alone leaves an offset; integral action removes it.

Exam use / trap: Type of system decides which inputs give zero error.

PID controller · P, I, D

Picture it as: Driving: P = how far from the lane centre, I = how long you have drifted, D = how fast you are drifting

How it matches: Combine all three for a smooth, accurate, quick correction.

Exam use / trap: D reduces overshoot; I removes offset.

Overshoot & settling · Mp, ts

Picture it as: Parking a car — overshoot the spot and come back

How it matches: Low damping = big overshoot and long settling.

Exam use / trap: Mp depends only on ζ.

Stability · poles in LHP

Picture it as: A ball in a BOWL (stable) vs on top of a hill (unstable)

How it matches: Disturbed, the stable ball returns; the unstable one runs away.

Exam use / trap: Any RHP pole → unstable.

Gain & phase margin · GM, PM

Picture it as: How far a car is from the cliff edge

How it matches: Safety distance before the loop starts to oscillate.

Exam use / trap: PM 30–60° gives good damping.

Transport lag · e^(−sT)

Picture it as: Shower with a long pipe — you turn the tap, the hot water arrives later

How it matches: Delay adds phase lag without changing gain → can destabilise.

Exam use / trap: Phase = −ωT rad.
1913:
14. Measurements

Ammeter · series, low R

Picture it as: A FLOW METER cut into the pipe

How it matches: Must not restrict the flow, so very low resistance.

Exam use / trap: Connected across a supply it acts as a short.

Voltmeter · parallel, high R

Picture it as: A PRESSURE GAUGE tapped across two points

How it matches: Must not leak water, so very high resistance.

Shunt (ammeter range extension) · Rsh =

Rm/(m − 1)

Picture it as: A BYPASS pipe taking most of the flow

How it matches: Only a known small share passes through the meter.

Multiplier (voltmeter range) · Rse = Rm(m − 1)

Picture it as: A long narrow pipe in series with the gauge

How it matches: Drops most of the pressure before the gauge.

Wheatstone bridge · R1R4 = R2R3

Picture it as: A BALANCE SCALE

How it matches: At balance no current flows through the galvanometer (the scale is level).

Exam use / trap: Null method → very accurate.

PMMC instrument · reads average

Picture it as: A weather-vane that points to the AVERAGE wind

How it matches: Pure AC averages to zero, so it reads 0 without a rectifier.

Exam use / trap: DC only (or with rectifier, scaled by 1.11).

Moving-iron instrument · reads rms

Picture it as: Two iron pieces that repel whichever way the current flows

How it matches: Deflection ∝ I², so it reads AC and DC (rms).

Energy meter · revolutions ∝ kWh

Picture it as: A water meter wheel counting litres

How it matches: The disc turns at a speed ∝ power, so total turns ∝ energy.

Exam use / trap: Meter constant = rev/kWh.

CRO · —

Picture it as: A pen drawing on moving paper

How it matches: Horizontal sweep = time, vertical deflection = signal.

Exam use / trap: Lissajous patterns compare frequencies.
1914:
15. Electromagnetic fields

Electric potential · V · volt

Picture it as: HEIGHT on a hill

How it matches: Equipotential lines are contour lines; moving along a contour costs no work.

Exam use / trap: Field lines always cross equipotentials at right angles.

Electric field · E · V/m

Picture it as: The SLOPE of the hill (field points downhill)

How it matches: E = −dV/dx: a steep slope is a strong field. Between parallel plates the slope is constant, E = V/d.

Exam use / trap: 1 kV across 1 mm = 10⁶ V/m.

Gauss's law (electric flux) · ∮D·dS = Q

Picture it as: Water flowing out of a closed bag = the tap inside it

How it matches: Total flux out of any closed surface equals the charge enclosed, whatever the bag's shape.

Exam use / trap: No charge inside → net flux zero.

Permittivity (dielectric) · ε = ε₀εr

Picture it as: A SPONGE that holds more water per unit pressure

How it matches: A dielectric lets the plates hold more charge per volt: C = εA/d grows with εr.

Exam use / trap: Inserting a dielectric (battery connected) raises Q; (battery removed) lowers V.

Magnetic field round a wire · B = μ₀I/(2πr)

Picture it as: WATER SWIRLING round a drain

How it matches: The swirl circles the current (right-hand grip) and weakens as 1/r.

Exam use / trap: Inside a solid wire B rises with r; outside it falls as 1/r.

Displacement current · Id = ε A dE/dt

Picture it as: Water pushing an ELASTIC MEMBRANE in a pipe

How it matches: No water crosses the membrane, yet flow continues on both sides — current 'through' a capacitor.

Exam use / trap: Makes Ampère's law hold at a capacitor (Maxwell).

Skin effect · δ = √(2/(ωμσ))

Picture it as: Rain RUN-OFF stays on the surface

How it matches: AC crowds to the outer skin of a conductor; higher frequency → thinner skin → higher Rac.

Exam use / trap: Hollow / stranded conductors at high current or frequency.

Method of images · —

Picture it as: A MIRROR

How it matches: A charge above a grounded plane acts as if an opposite charge sits at its mirror point below.

Exam use / trap: Force on the charge = q²/(4πε₀(2h)²).

Electromagnetic wave · η₀ = 377 Ω

Picture it as: A STADIUM WAVE

How it matches: E and H hand energy back and forth while the pattern travels at c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀).

Exam use / trap: E/H = 377 Ω in free space.
1915:
16. Digital electronics

AND / OR gate · Y = A·B, A + B

Picture it as: Two SWITCHES in series / in parallel

How it matches: Lamp lights only if both series switches close (AND) or if either parallel switch closes (OR).

Exam use / trap: NAND and NOR alone can build any gate (universal).

Inverter · Y = Ā

Picture it as: A SEE-SAW

How it matches: One end up means the other end down.

Exam use / trap: Two inverters in series give the input back.

Latch / flip-flop · 1 bit of memory

Picture it as: A LIGHT SWITCH that stays where you leave it

How it matches: It keeps its state after your hand leaves — memory.

Exam use / trap: SR: S = R = 1 is the forbidden input.

T (toggle) flip-flop · Q⁺ = Q̄ when T = 1

Picture it as: A PUSH-BUTTON lamp: press on, press off

How it matches: Each clock with T = 1 flips the state — a divide-by-2 circuit.

Exam use / trap: n toggling flip-flops divide the clock by 2ⁿ.

Clock · fclk

Picture it as: A CONDUCTOR'S BATON

How it matches: Every synchronous flip-flop changes only on the beat.

Exam use / trap: Synchronous counter: all stages share one clock.

Ripple counter · delay = n·tpd

Picture it as: DOMINOES falling one after another

How it matches: Each stage waits for the previous one, so delays add up.

Exam use / trap: Max clock ≈ 1/(n·tpd).

Shift register · SISO, SIPO, PISO, PIPO

Picture it as: A BUCKET BRIGADE

How it matches: Each clock passes every bit one place along the line.

Exam use / trap: n-bit serial-in → output after n clocks.

Multiplexer / demultiplexer · 2ⁿ inputs, n select

lines

Picture it as: A RAILWAY JUNCTION

How it matches: Select lines set the points: one of many tracks joins the main line (MUX), or the main line feeds one of many (DEMUX).

Exam use / trap: A 2ⁿ:1 MUX can realise any n-variable function.

Tri-state buffer · 0, 1, high-Z

Picture it as: A door that can be OPEN, CLOSED or TAKEN AWAY

How it matches: High-Z disconnects the output so many devices can share one bus.

Exam use / trap: Used on data buses.
1916:
17. Signals & DSP

Impulse response · h(t), h[n]

Picture it as: CLAP ONCE and record the hall's reply

How it matches: The reply to one sharp clap describes the whole room (LTI system).

Exam use / trap: Knowing h gives the output for any input.

Convolution · y = x * h

Picture it as: ECHOES in a hall

How it matches: The output is every past input, each followed by its own echo pattern, all added up.

Exam use / trap: Convolution in time = multiplication in frequency.

Fourier series / spectrum · harmonics

Picture it as: A PRISM splitting white light into colours

How it matches: Any periodic wave splits into sine waves of f, 2f, 3f …

Exam use / trap: Square wave → only odd harmonics.

Sampling & aliasing · fs ≥ 2fmax

Picture it as: FILM FRAMES — wagon wheels that seem to turn backwards

How it matches: Too few frames per turn and the wheel's true speed is disguised as a slower one.

Exam use / trap: Alias at |f − k·fs|.

Low-pass filter · fc = 1/(2πRC)

Picture it as: CAR SUSPENSION smoothing out bumps

How it matches: Slow changes pass, fast jolts are absorbed.

Exam use / trap: RC = 1 s → fc ≈ 0.16 Hz.

Stability (BIBO) · poles in LHP / inside |z| = 1

Picture it as: A BALL IN A BOWL vs a ball on a HILLTOP

How it matches: Disturb the bowl and the ball settles (stable); on the hilltop it rolls away (unstable).

Exam use / trap: One pole in the right half-plane → unstable.

Delay z⁻¹ · y[n] = x[n − 1]

Picture it as: A one-step QUEUE

How it matches: Each sample waits one tick before moving on.

Exam use / trap: z⁻ᵏ = delay of k samples.

Causality · h(t) = 0 for t < 0

Picture it as: No one can REPLY BEFORE BEING ASKED

How it matches: A real-time system cannot use future inputs.

Exam use / trap: Ideal (brick-wall) filters are non-causal.
1917:
18. Communication

Carrier & modulation · fc ≫ fm

Picture it as: A TRUCK carrying the message as cargo

How it matches: The low-frequency message rides on a high-frequency carrier that antennas can launch.

Exam use / trap: Antenna length ≈ λ/2 — impossible at audio frequencies.

AM vs FM · m, β

Picture it as: LOUDNESS change vs PITCH change (a siren)

How it matches: AM varies the carrier's size; FM varies its frequency.

Exam use / trap: FM resists noise because noise mostly disturbs amplitude.

Bandwidth & capacity · C = B log₂(1 + SNR)

Picture it as: LANES on a highway

How it matches: More lanes (bandwidth) and a clearer road (SNR) carry more traffic (bits per second).

Exam use / trap: SNR 1000 (30 dB), B = 3 kHz → C ≈ 30 kb/s.

Noise & SNR · SNR (dB)

Picture it as: TALKING in a noisy room

How it matches: What matters is how much louder the voice is than the crowd.

Exam use / trap: Noise figure F = SNRin/SNRout ≥ 1.

FDM vs TDM · —

Picture it as: RADIO STATIONS on different channels vs people TAKING TURNS to speak

How it matches: FDM shares the band at once; TDM shares the time slot by slot.

Exam use / trap: TDM is natural for digital (PCM) signals.

Superheterodyne receiver · IF = 455 kHz (AM)

Picture it as: TRANSLATING every language into one common language first

How it matches: Every station is shifted to one fixed IF so one well-tuned amplifier does the work.

Exam use / trap: Image frequency = fs + 2·IF.

Pre-emphasis / de-emphasis · 75 µs (FM)

Picture it as: SPEAKING the soft high notes louder before a noisy line

How it matches: High audio frequencies are boosted at the transmitter and cut back at the receiver, cutting the noise with them.

Exam use / trap: Improves FM SNR at high audio frequencies.

Antenna · λ/2 dipole

Picture it as: A TUNING FORK

How it matches: It radiates best at the frequency its length matches.

Exam use / trap: λ = c/f: 100 MHz → 3 m, half-wave dipole ≈ 1.5 m.
1918:
19. Utilization of electrical energy

Luminous intensity · illuminance · cd · lux =

lm/m²

Picture it as: A TORCH's brightness in one direction · RAIN per square metre

How it matches: Candela is how strongly a source shines one way; lux is how much light lands on each square metre.

Exam use / trap: E = I/d² (inverse square) and E = I cos θ/d² (cosine law).

Inverse-square law · E ∝ 1/d²

Picture it as: SPRAY PAINT thinning out with distance

How it matches: Twice as far → the same paint covers 4 times the area.

Exam use / trap: Lamp raised from 2 m to 4 m → illuminance ¼.

Resistance heating · P = I²R

Picture it as: FRICTION in a narrow pipe

How it matches: Forcing current through resistance turns energy into heat.

Exam use / trap: Nichrome elements: high ρ, no oxidation.

Induction heating · eddy currents

Picture it as: WHIRLPOOLS stirred inside the metal

How it matches: An AC coil induces swirling currents that heat the work-piece from inside; higher f → shallower heating.

Exam use / trap: Used for surface hardening and melting.

Dielectric heating · P ∝ f V² tan δ

Picture it as: MOLECULES jostling back and forth

How it matches: Polar molecules twist with the field many million times a second and warm up (like a microwave oven).

Exam use / trap: Heats insulators — wood, plastics, food.

Train speed–time curve · accelerate, free-run,

coast, brake

Picture it as: A BUS between two stops

How it matches: Speed up, cruise, roll on, then brake — the area under the curve is the distance.

Exam use / trap: Shorter runs → no free-running part (trapezoidal curve).

Regenerative braking · motor → generator

Picture it as: A PUMP run backwards as a TURBINE downhill

How it matches: The motor slows the train and sends energy back to the supply.

Exam use / trap: Works only when the back EMF exceeds the supply voltage.

Battery capacity · Ah · Wh = V × Ah

Picture it as: A WATER TANK: size = Ah, height = volts

How it matches: Stored energy = how much water × how high it sits.

Exam use / trap: 12 V, 100 Ah = 1.2 kWh.
